episodes.title: West Carroll Parish lynchings of August 1890
episodes.lists: None (not in Beck–Tolnay, Seguin–Rigby or HAL)
episodes.summary: The West Carroll Parish lynchings of August 1890 were the reported killings by lynching of two Black men and one white man in West Carroll Parish, Louisiana, on a Monday night in mid-August 1890. Each man was accused of a separate offense, and the only known account is a two-sentence item from the local Carroll Banner, reprinted in a Lake Charles paper.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching at Jacksonville, Alabama
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching at Jacksonville, Alabama, was an August 1890 effort by a mob of about 1,000 people to seize and hang an unnamed Black man held by the sheriff in Calhoun County, who was accused of having tried to rape the young daughter of a white man, Benjamin Carpenter. The sheriff moved the prisoner first to Anniston and then farther south, while the mob followed, chartered a special train and cut the wires. Wire reports predicted a "first-class hanging," but no confirmation that the man was killed appears in the coverage, and a brief Texas report that he had been lynched appears to compress the same dispatch.

episodes.title: Lynching of Jim Robinson
episodes.summary: The lynching of Jim Robinson was the hanging of a Black man at Shaw, Mississippi, on the night of Tuesday, August 26, 1890. Robinson had been accused of outraging the 8-year-old daughter of Henry Meyers near Shaw earlier that week. The killing drew only brief notice in two Mississippi weeklies, both of which treated the accusation as established fact.

episodes.title: Police beating of George Bailey
episodes.summary: The police beating of George Bailey was an alleged assault in Washington, D.C., in late July or early August 1890, in which Officer John H. Trammell of the Second Precinct was charged with clubbing Bailey, a Black man, while arresting him. District Attorney Armes dropped the assault charge against the officer, and Black residents took up the case at protest meetings against police violence that August.

episodes.title: Onancock wharf riot
episodes.summary: The Onancock wharf riot was a fight on August 17, 1890, at the steamboat wharf in Onancock, Accomack County, Virginia, between white townsmen and Black excursionists from Baltimore boarding the steamer Helen after a camp meeting. Stones, bricks and pistols were used, and two papers reported at least three Black passengers shot or struck, while a Baltimore German paper said no one was known to be wounded. No arrests were reported, and the Richmond Dispatch presented the affair as "A NEGRO OUTRAGE."

episodes.title: Killing of Julian Jones
episodes.summary: The killing of Julian Jones was the fatal shooting of a Black farm hand by Raleigh policeman William E. Hogue on Hargett street in Raleigh, North Carolina, on August 2, 1890. Hogue, who said he fired while making an arrest, was charged with murder on a Black man's warrant, jailed without bail and indicted in September. Black residents packed the hearings, and the city kept its militia company ready.

episodes.title: Carbon Iron Works strike against Black puddlers
episodes.summary: The Carbon Iron Works strike against Black puddlers was a walkout by the employees of the Carbon Iron Works in Pittsburg, Pennsylvania, on 4 August 1890, called after the company put Black men to work in its idle puddling department. Between 300 and 500 men left the works, and wire reports said the strikers threatened violence against the Black workers. Papers across the country carried the story as a strike caused by the hiring of "negroes" or "colored men."

episodes.title: Lynching of William Waters
episodes.summary: The lynching of William Waters, also reported as William Walters, took place near Mayview, Lafayette County, Missouri, on August 29, 1890, when a crowd hanged a Black youth accused of murdering E. F. Parker, a Mayview merchant, that morning. Seized within hours, Waters was said by his captors to have confessed under a noose and was hanged that night after they hid him from county officers. Wire dispatches presented the case as a murder and lynching completed in one day, and a report on his funeral described indignation among Black residents of the county.

episodes.title: Safford ballot box incident
episodes.summary: The Safford ballot box incident was an episode in Dallas County, Alabama, on the afternoon of the state election of August 4, 1890, in which a few armed men from Selma, sent out on the sheriff's orders, dispersed a crowd of Black people at the Safford polling place and carried off the ballot box. No one was reported hurt, and the only account, a Selma dispatch, claimed the crowd had planned to seize the box. Newspapers across the country carried the dispatch inside reports of a Democratic sweep and light Black turnout, and a Kansas paper reprinted it to dispute it.

episodes.title: Lynching of William Beaver
episodes.summary: The lynching of William Beaver took place near Warren, Bradley County, Arkansas, on the night of August 10, 1890, when an armed mob took the young Black man from the county sheriff and hanged him. Beaver had been accused of attempting to assault Inez Abernathy, the daughter of the man he lived with, and a Black girl. An Arkansas City dispatch carried the story to papers across the country within days, many of them under headlines that endorsed the killing.

episodes.title: Pocahontas moonshiner raid
episodes.summary: The Pocahontas moonshiner raid was an armed incursion into Pocahontas, Virginia, on a Sunday in late July 1890, apparently July 20, by a band of about twenty men from West Virginia who got drunk and fired on passers-by. Two Black residents, one of them Charles Smith, were seriously wounded before town officers fought off the band, captured two of its members and drove the rest back across the state line. Newspapers as far away as Kansas, South Carolina and Georgia carried the story as a moonshiners' raid and a "border war."

episodes.title: Lynching of Thomas Woodward
episodes.summary: The lynching of Thomas Woodward took place about midnight on Saturday, August 16, 1890, when a mob took Woodward, a Black prisoner, from the jail at Humboldt, Tennessee, and hanged him. Woodward was accused of being one of three Black men who had assaulted and robbed a man named J. A. Greer two nights earlier. The killing was reported mainly through a brief wire dispatch, later picked up in columns of Afro-American news.

episodes.title: Lynching of John Brown
episodes.summary: The lynching of John Brown took place on August 4, 1890, near Anderson, Texas, when a crowd of citizens seized Brown, a Black prisoner accused of raping a white girl, from the keeping of Sheriff Scott and hanged him. According to the reports, his body was then filled with bullets, and the papers stated that he had confessed before he died. Besides Texas papers, a United Press dispatch carried the news to North Carolina, Virginia and Oregon.

episodes.title: Lynching of Henry Jessies
episodes.summary: The lynching of Henry Jessies, a Black man also reported as Henry Jessee and as John Jones, took place near Dickinsonville in Russell County, Virginia, on the night of Saturday, August 2, 1890, when a posse of about a hundred men hanged him from a tree and shot his body. He was accused of sexually assaulting a white woman that afternoon, and one account said his body was found the next day with thirty-six bullet holes. Virginia papers reported the killing under headlines calling him a "negro fiend," while a Roanoke dispatch noted that his brother claimed he could identify the lynchers.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Will Johnson
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Will Johnson was a mob threat in August 1890 against a Black boy, also named as John or Joe Johnson, held in the jail at Opelika, Alabama, after he was accused of burglary, of wounding several men and of killing Jenkins Moore, a merchant and justice of the peace at Gold Hill. A mob threatened the jail but made no attack after the sheriff placed a guard around it. Papers across the country carried the story, stressing the boy's reported age of fourteen and casting him as a "desperado."

episodes.title: Whitecapping of John Baxter
episodes.summary: The whitecapping of John Baxter was a night attack at Smithfield, Pennsylvania, in August 1890, in which eight or ten masked men whipped Baxter, a Black man, with cowhides after he ignored a notice signed "White Caps" ordering him to leave the community. The notice had been sent to Baxter and Mrs. Jennie Smith, a white woman living with him, and she fled before the band arrived. White papers from Pennsylvania to Washington and Tennessee printed the Uniontown dispatch, one under the headline "White Caps Are Sometimes Right."

episodes.title: Lynching of John Henderson
episodes.summary: The lynching of John Henderson took place in the early hours of August 21, 1890, when masked men took Henderson, a Black prisoner, from the Woodford County jail at Versailles, Kentucky, and hanged him from a tree. He had been accused of killing Gilbert Satterwhite, a white farmer, near Midway three days earlier. A coroner's jury found that he died at the hands of persons unknown, and a Kentucky paper condemned the lynching and the jailer who allowed it.

episodes.title: Lynching of Henderson Fox
episodes.summary: The lynching of Henderson Fox took place at Trenton, Gibson County, Tennessee, in mid-August 1890, when a mob reported as about 200 men took Fox, a Black prisoner, from the county jail and hanged him. Fox was accused of raping a white girl, Annie Dowling, the previous May, and had been brought back from the Indian Territory days before. White papers in Tennessee and beyond carried the news, most of them stating the accusation as fact.

episodes.title: Bangor crap-game raid
episodes.summary: The Bangor crap-game raid was a raid by Sheriff A. H. Morris of Blount County and a posse on a gathering of Black dice players at Bangor, Alabama, early on a Sunday morning in August 1890, in which a Black man named Jim Thomas was killed. Several other men were slightly wounded and the sheriff received a flesh wound, and the story circulated as a brief wire item in papers in Tennessee, Kentucky, West Virginia and Ohio.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Edmund Morrison
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Edmund Morrison followed the shooting of Henry Hunter, a young man of Athens, Georgia, at Carter's camp on the Georgia, Carolina and Northern railroad on the night of August 16, 1890, of which Morrison, a Black laborer at the camp, was accused. About 100 men with bloodhounds hunted Morrison, and wire reports carried across the country stated that he would be lynched when caught. He was instead captured by a sheriff and lodged in the Augusta jail to protect him from a mob, and in September he was tried, convicted and sentenced to hang.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Miles Mayo
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Miles Mayo took place at Roslyn, Washington, in early August 1890, when talk of lynching followed Mayo's arrest for stabbing a white liveryman in a quarrel over a horse. Town officials took Mayo, a Black man, out of the Roslyn jail to Ellensburg for safe keeping, and he was not harmed. Papers on the Pacific coast treated the case as a near "race war" because Black residents declared they would avenge Mayo if he were lynched.

episodes.title: Shooting of Greely McDowell
episodes.summary: The shooting of Greely McDowell took place in Rutherfordton, North Carolina, on August 1, 1890, when the town marshal shot McDowell, a Black man he was trying to arrest, and then fired into a crowd of Black residents. McDowell was seriously wounded and about three other Black men were reported hurt, but no deaths were reported. White newspapers in the South and beyond reported the affair as a near "race war" and a "riot" by a Black mob, although a local dispatch said there was "No excitement."

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of John Jordan
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of John Jordan occurred at Frankfort, Kentucky, in August 1890, when Jordan, a Black man held in jail there on a charge of assaulting a little girl, was threatened with lynching. Officials placed an extra guard at the jail, and no attack on Jordan was reported. The episode is known only from a short wire item reprinted in out-of-state news digests.

episodes.title: Lynching of Willis Alexander
episodes.summary: The lynching of Willis Alexander was the killing of a 17-year-old Black youth near Baton Rouge, in East Baton Rouge Parish, Louisiana, on the night of August 21, 1890. He had been accused of attempting to assault an eleven-year-old white girl, and his body was found the next day hanging from a tree beside a road. The news reached papers across the country as a short wire item and a one-line digest entry.

episodes.title: Lynching of Jim Winget
episodes.summary: The lynching of Jim Winget was the hanging of a Black man, Jim Winget, also known as Jim Cason, by unidentified men in Bossier Parish, Louisiana, on a Tuesday night in mid-August 1890. Winget was taken from his house and hanged in a yard a mile and a half away, and he was said to have been a witness in a pending murder case. The killing is known from a single short paragraph in the Shreveport Caucasian, reprinted in the Bossier Banner.

episodes.title: Aberdeen church ambush
episodes.summary: The Aberdeen church ambush was the shooting of a party of Black churchgoers from ambush near Aberdeen, Mississippi, on the night of Sunday, August 3, 1890. Susan Henry was killed instantly, and her husband, named Ben Henry in most dispatches, was seriously wounded. The coverage did not identify the attacker, but wire dispatches carried the story to papers from Pennsylvania to Arizona within a week, under headlines that ranged from condemnation to mockery of the victims.

episodes.title: Dublin Republican convention incident
episodes.summary: The Dublin Republican convention incident was the ordering out of town of two Black delegates from Thurber who had come to Dublin, Erath County, Texas, for a Republican county convention called for August 16, 1890. All accounts agreed that the delegates were told to leave, but they differed on who gave the order, whether the delegates left, and why the convention failed. A report from Thurber calling the affair an outrage drew public denials from a Dublin citizens' meeting and from the town's mayor, and the county convention met at Dublin ten days later.

episodes.title: Greensboro police whipping (1890)
episodes.summary: The Greensboro police whipping was the whipping of a number of Black people by a policeman in Greensboro, North Carolina, in early August 1890, as punishment for fighting. It is known from a single line in the Asheville Daily Citizen, which described the policeman as "properly delegated" and gave no names, number of victims or exact date.

episodes.title: Pacific Avenue police shooting (Dallas, 1890)
episodes.summary: The Pacific Avenue police shooting took place in Dallas, Texas, at about 1 a.m. on August 1, 1890, when Officer Ragland of the city police chased an unnamed Black man from beneath a shed on Pacific avenue and fired five shots at him as he ran. The man outran the officer and escaped, and no wound was reported. The only known account, a Dallas special to the Fort Worth Daily Gazette, told the shooting as a comic item in a column on petty theft.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Tom Chambers
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of Tom Chambers was a night attack by a white "vigilance committee" on a Black man at his home on the Tennessee side of Fulton in August 1890. Chambers fought off the band with a hatchet and a knife, and a rope with a hangman's knot found the next morning was taken as the purpose of the visit.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Lawson Simril
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of Lawson Simril took place in Ebernezer Township, apparently in South Carolina, on Wednesday, 6 August 1890, when a crowd of neighbors seized and bound Simril, a Black man accused of entering a young woman's room at night, and resolved to execute him. A local man persuaded the crowd to let the law take its course, and Simril was jailed the next morning to await trial. The Lexington Dispatch reported it as a "Narrow Escape From Lynching."

episodes.title: Police shooting of Chris Brooks
episodes.summary: The police shooting of Chris Brooks took place in Wilmington, Delaware, in August 1890, when Officer Sherer used his revolver while arresting Brooks, a Black man charged with stealing chickens, and wounded him in the leg. The shooting became known when the city solicitor mentioned it at Brooks's hearing in the Municipal Court on August 18, and the case was postponed for a week so that the wound could be treated.

episodes.title: Shooting of George Carter
episodes.summary: The shooting of George Carter took place in King George County, Virginia, in August 1890, when Randolph Inscoe, a white man, shot Carter, a Black man, after a quarrel and left him with what the papers called a mortal wound. Inscoe was arrested, examined before a magistrate and released on bail to await the next term of the County Court. Richmond dispatches attributed the quarrel to "political talk and impudence on the part of the negro" in a hotly contested congressional district, while a later report from the county seat traced it to a dispute over hauling wood.

episodes.title: Rome sidewalk clash (1890)
episodes.doubt: two white attackers and a crowd urging them on; whether a group acted is for the dossier
episodes.summary: The Rome sidewalk clash was a street confrontation on the afternoon of August 23, 1890, in Rome, Georgia, in which two white men struck and knocked down a Black man after a sidewalk collision while a white crowd urged them on. Other Black men joined the fight, police made one or two arrests, and a Rome dispatch described it as a near "serious conflict between whites and blacks."

episodes.title: Americus whipping and ax-handle assault (1890)
episodes.doubt: lone private attackers, two separate acts
episodes.summary: The Americus whipping and ax-handle assault took place on Saturday, 23 August 1890, in Americus, Georgia, when a white woman whipped a Black girl and her husband, a storekeeper, struck the girl's father on the head with an ax handle. Four or five warrants were issued two days later, and the episode is known only from a single paragraph in the Savannah Morning News.

episodes.title: Whitecapping of Clifford Williams
episodes.summary: The whitecapping of Clifford Williams was a night raid and written warning against a Black man near Bryant Station, Saline County, Arkansas, in August 1890. About twenty armed men seized him to see whether the women of a white household would identify him as an accused assailant, and released him when they did not. A notice signed "Committee" then ordered him to leave within ten days, and he moved away.
